title: In deed and in truth (1 John 3:11–18)
hookLine: love not in word only but in deed

lines: A BANK ACCOUNT, AND A NEED.
cards: A heart emoji takes half a second. A sympathy post takes ten. Driving across town with soup takes an afternoon.
All three can be sincere, but only one is warm when it arrives. For days now, First John has circled love: old, new, the love that names believers children of God. Today he gets very practical.
He reaches back to Cain and Abel, then asks a question about a bank account and a neighbor in need. A letter that can sometimes float comes down to earth.

teach.h: LOVE ONE ANOTHER, FROM THE BEGINNING.
teach.b: In the King James Bible: "For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another."

Then the counterexample, from the first pages of Genesis: don't be like Cain, who killed his brother. Whoever hates his brother, the writer says, is a murderer at heart. Hatred is the seed; Cain shows what it grows into.
So what does love look like? Not a feeling first. A shape.

teach.h: HE LAID DOWN HIS LIFE FOR US.
teach.b: "Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren." For Christians, the cross is the measure of love.
Then, right away, the writer brings it from the heroic to the everyday. Laying down a life is rare.
But: "whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him?" Bowels of compassion sounds odd to us.
The Greek word means the inner organs, the gut, where feeling was felt. We still say a gut feeling. The picture is someone who sees a need, feels that tug inside, and shuts it off.
Then the line the passage builds to: "My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth." In deed: something done. In truth: something real, not a performance.

That closes a week from the end of James into First John: pray for one another, what we have touched, God is light, the old new commandment, little children, what manner of love, and in deed and in truth.

how: Christians organizing meal trains, collections and visiting sometimes quote 1 John 3:18, and churches read it alongside James 2 on faith and works.

a quick hunch about whether to trust someone
a sudden fear that warns you of danger

p: not in word, neither in tongue

s: 'bowels of compassion' meant the gut was seen as the seat of feeling
we still talk about a gut feeling.
the writer says love is mainly a warm feeling
he defines it by a deed: he laid down his life for us.
the writer brings love down to everyday needs
seeing a brother in need and not shutting up compassion.

games.q: you have plenty, and you see a friend in real need. you feel the tug. what does the letter ask?
o: send warm words and move on.
open your hand and help, in deed and in truth.
games.why: "how dwelleth the love of God in him?" the writer asks of anyone who shuts up compassion. "let us not love in word... but in deed and in truth."

practice: Think of a need you've seen this week that tugged at you, someone tired, short of money, lonely or sick, and notice whether you shut the tug off, and why, without blame.
Then picture one small deed you could actually do about it, step by step, until you can see it clearly. If you pray, ask for the courage to follow through.

wordCard.voice: Gut feeling. First John's old image for compassion, the inner organs, the gut, where feeling was felt: a tug inside that love doesn't shut off.

orig.note: Greek: inner organs, the gut, and so compassion. the KJV renders it bowels of compassion.

carryVoice: Your line: not in word only. Love, in this letter, has a shape. Six hundred eighty-six days now.
